artwork_clues.meaning: The front window's split() label points to the contract operation involved in the exploit. It does not refer to the later Ethereum and Ethereum Classic fork.
Nested windows and the paper trail visualise recursion. Their repetition conveys the same operation happening again inside an unfinished call; the interface and receipts are invented.
The cabinet and ≈27 DAYS display recall the temporary withdrawal restriction. The number is an approximate period reported during the attack, not a precise countdown to the hard fork.
The plate reads 0x304a…3490, abbreviating the child DAO address named in the contemporary alert. Its correctly retained beginning and ending anchor the fictional machinery to the historical record.

cards.interpretation: Fictional young-Vitalik-inspired response scene. The room, terminal, nested windows, receipts, locked Ether cabinet, posture and response actions are invented symbolic staging, not documented actions or an identification of the attacker. The DAO application exploit is distinct from an Ethereum consensus failure. The split() contract function and 17 June exploit are distinct from the 20 July hard fork. The approximate 27-day display is a reported temporary withdrawal restriction, not a precise fork countdown.
cards.card_size_readability_note: Four clue areas are unobstructed in the reviewed card. The address and small nested labels are very fine at physical size; no unaided readability or phone-camera claim is made.

historical_versions.creator: ETHEREUM
historical_versions.interpretation: Fictional sealed vaults visualise The DAO exploit. A one-way violet stream depicts ETH diverted into the locked child DAO. A small amber loop at the SPLIT control represents recursive calls, not funds returned to The DAO. Enlarged fictional engineers convey urgency. The receiver display references the approximate 27-day withdrawal restriction reported during the attack. No actual physical building, identifiable attacker, Ethereum consensus breach or later July fork is depicted.

artwork_clues.meaning: The wooden sign identifies the currency used to buy ether. The cliff-top stall is a visual shorthand for the online sale, not a historical location.
The small calendar shows 22 JUL 2014 and 42 DAYS, fixing the opening date and the length of the sale beside the collection chest.
The paper in the visitor's hand carries BTC-to-ETH and ALLOCATION wording. It stands for a recorded purchase awaiting a network that had yet to launch.
Cranes and exposed scaffolding surround a giant octahedral structure. Ethereum's familiar shape identifies the project; the incomplete buildings picture the development still to come.
The device's screen and two physical buttons reference independent review and confirmation. The simplified "Confirm?" display is illustrative, not a verified July 2014 firmware screen.

Blank numbered lines recall the need for an offline wallet backup. No secret words are shown, and the visible line count is not presented as a verified 2014 standard. The two loose sheets remain deliberately blank.

The warm upper-left lamp and red computer glow make the contrast between owner control and a threatening host visible. The person, room and warning screen are an invented scene, not a documented launch photograph.

sources.title: Ethereum Foundation: Frontier is coming
sources.supports: Barebone developer release, initial 5,000 gas-per-block thawing limit preventing transactions.

sources.title: Ethereum gas and fees: technical overview
sources.supports: Gas measures computational effort; gas prices quoted in gwei. Used only for stable unit distinction, not modern base-fee/tip mechanics or any claimed 2015 fee.

artwork_clues.meaning: The gantry names Ethereum's first live release. Its placement in a fictional industrial city makes a software milestone part of the landscape.
The illuminated 0 at the central junction represents the genesis block, the network's starting point. The physical module is an invented visual symbol.
BLOCK GAS LIMIT 5,000 records Frontier's initial thawing restriction. It is a limit on gas per block, not a gas price or a pressure reading.

Concrete panels, open floors and scaffolding turn Ethereum's diamond into architecture. They express the developer-focused release's unfinished state. The city also echoes card 028, The Ether Sale, carrying its imagined future into the first live network.
